messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: problem using a function inside ddply
parts:
Hi:

The trick when calling a function in connection with a **ply()
function is that the input argument to the function should be of the
same type as the input specified by **ply (in this case, d) and the
output object from the function should be the same type as the output
type specified by **ply. [The exception to this rule applies to
*lply().] In your case, ddply => your function should have a data
frame input and a data frame output. Your function input a data frame
but output an atomic vector. You should do the transform inside the
function and then output the transformed data frame, as follows:

df$democracy.l1 <- res0[-length(res0)]
df
}

Notice that everything is done inside the function. An alternative
version using pure plyr tools is the following:

my.lag2 <- function(df){
df <- arrange(df, year.x)
res0 <- c(NA,df$democracy)
mutate(df, democracy.l1 = res0[-length(res0)])
}

arrange() is the plyr equivalent of df[order(df$blah), ]; mutate() is
the plyr equivalent of transform, with the added feature that you can
define a new variable in mutate() and then use it in subsequent
variable definitions within the same call (a very handy feature, BTW).
Then,

u <- ddply(merged5, .(country.x), my.lag1)
v <- ddply(merged5, .(country.x), my.lag2)
identical(u, v)
# [1] TRUE
head(u) # to check that it worked.

The general form of a ddply() call is

ddply(dataFrame, .(grouping variables), function, extra arguments to function)

This is analogous to the apply family of functions, which allows one
to add optional arguments after the function is declared; e.g.,
apply(mat, 1, mean, na.rm = TRUE). It's easy to forget this point (I
certainly have), so I've found it convenient to do as much as possible
inside the function body and return (in this case) a data frame to
ddply(). Hopefully this point clarifies why your ddply() function call
didn't work and gives you a little more insight into its syntax.

Side note: Thank you for using dput(), but...some subscribers read
e-mail through their cell phones and a submission of the length you
provided might not enamor you to such users because of bandwidth
limitations. I would kindly suggest that if you want to make available
a data set of this length, put it up on a web site instead (in dput()
form if you wish, but other formats are fine [and probably preferred
since R has several functions to read files directly from the web])
and include the link in your mail or, alternatively, attach the
data/dput to the e-mail as a separate text file.

Just in case...to read dput() output from an external file, use
dget('dputfile').

HTH,
Dennis

On Sun, Nov 27, 2011 at 6:42 PM, Antonio Pedro
<ramos.gra...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I just wrote a function to give lagged values of my predictors. It is
> very simple an apparently is working well. Now I need to use ddply to
> apply this function to my data set, but country by country. This is
> supposed to be an easy task but something is not working and I cannot
> figure it out why. I would really appreciated any help. Best,
> Antonio.
>
>
> #===========================================================================================
> my.lag1 <- function(df){
>     df <- df[order(df$year.x),]
>     res0 <- c(NA,df$democracy)
>     res1 <- res0[-length(res0)]
>     return(res1)
> }
>
>> z <- ddply(merged5, .(country.x),transform,democracy.l1 = my.lag1(merged))
> Error in data.frame(list(country.x = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
> 1L,  :
>  arguments imply differing number of rows: 41, 7033
>
>> z$democracy.l1 <- ddply(merged5, .(country.x), my.lag1)
> Error in list_to_dataframe(res, attr(.data, "split_labels")) :
>  Results do not have equal lengths
>>
>
>
